a: apart from him not a single thing came to exist. What came to exist
p: Goes with 1:4. Early writers ended the sentence before "what came to exist"; later ones after it.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28. Metzger reports this division in the manuscripts that punctuate here (Papyrus 75 by a corrector, Ephraemi, Bezae) and in nearly all writers of the 100s and 200s (Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Origen)
readings.orig: οὐδὲ ἕν. ὃ γέγονεν ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν
readings.en: not one thing. What has come to be, in him was life
readings.plain: apart from him not a single thing came to exist. What came to exist

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV "without him was not any thing made that was made"), followed by most English Bibles; Metzger names later Greek writers such as Chrysostom
readings.orig: οὐδὲ ἓν ὃ γέγονεν. ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν
readings.en: not one thing that has come to be. In him was life
readings.plain: apart from him not a single thing came to exist of all that exists.

why: The oldest manuscripts have almost no punctuation, so this is a choice between early readings of the text, not between different words. SBLGNT and NA28 follow the earliest writers. Many scholars, Metzger among them, prefer the other division, because John often starts a sentence with "in" and because "what came to exist in him was life" is hard to explain.
b: With the early division, the sense is that everything that came into being had life in the Word. With the later one, the Word himself has life. Some think the later division spread after the 300s, when teachers on both sides of the Arian debate used the verse.

p: Goes with 1:3: "What came to exist in him was life" or a new sentence, "In him was life."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and the earliest writers (see 1:3)
readings.orig: ὃ γέγονεν ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν
readings.en: what has come to be, in him was life

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV); most English Bibles

why: This entry goes with the one on 1:3: see there.

a: Their birth came not from blood, not from fleshly desire, not from a man's decision, but from God.
p: Every Greek manuscript says "they were born." A few Latin witnesses say "he was born," of Jesus' virgin birth.

readings.w: All editions (SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine, Textus Receptus); Metzger reports no Greek manuscript with the singular
readings.plain: Their birth came not from blood, not from fleshly desire, not from a man's decision, but from God.

readings.w: The Old Latin Codex Veronensis and the Latin of Irenaeus and Tertullian, as reported by Metzger
readings.plain: His birth came not from blood, not from fleshly desire, not from a man's decision, but from God.

why: The plural has all the Greek evidence. The singular is very old, but it looks like a change made to find Jesus' virgin birth in the prologue. A few scholars have argued that the singular is original.

p: The KJV begins "And of his fulness have all we received." Most editions begin with "For."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "And")

why: "For" ties the verse to 1:14, "full of grace and truth": we know he was full, because we have all received from his fullness. "And" is a smoother link that copyists could easily make, since 1:15 interrupts.

t: "The only Son" or "the only one, God"?
p: The editions split. SBLGNT and NA28 read "only God"; the Tyndale House GNT, the Byzantine text and the KJV read "the only Son."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles. As reported by Metzger: Papyrus 66, Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Vaticanus, Ephraemi (first hand), L; Papyrus 75 and a corrector of Sinaiticus add "the"
readings.en: only-born God, the only one, God

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "the only begotten Son"). As reported by Metzger: Alexandrinus, a corrector of Ephraemi, Washington (supplement), Θ, Ψ, families 1 and 13, most later manuscripts, the Old Latin, Vulgate and Curetonian Syriac

why: "God" has the oldest witnesses, including both early papyri, and it is the harder reading: a copyist could easily change the unusual "only God" to the familiar "only Son" (as in 3:16, 18; 1 John 4:9). The Tyndale House editors, and scholars such as Bart Ehrman, judge "Son" original: it fits John's usage, and Ehrman argues "God" was brought in to oppose teachers who denied Christ's divinity. Others reply that the theology of "God" is already in 1:1.
b: In Greek manuscripts the two words were written as abbreviations, ΘΣ for God and ΥΣ for Son, so they look alike, which made a slip easy either way. Even with "God", monogenēs may stand alone ("the only one") with "God" beside it, as this translation takes it, or as an adjective, "the only God". The verse frames the prologue: the Word who "was God" (1:1) is God who makes God known (1:18).

a: the one who comes after me.
t: A longer saying in the KJV
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add words from 1:15 and 1:30: "who is preferred before me."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.plain: the one who comes after me.

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "He it is, who coming after me is preferred before me")
readings.orig: αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ ὀπίσω μου ἐρχόμενος, ὃς ἔμπροσθέν μου γέγονεν
readings.en: he is the one coming after me, who has moved ahead of me
readings.plain: he is the one who comes after me, who has gone ahead of me.

why: All the critical editions print the shorter text, which Metzger reports from the earliest manuscripts. Copyists filled out John's words here to match 1:15 and 1:30, a common kind of change.

p: The KJV reads "Bethabara," a place Origen preferred because he could not find a Bethany by the Jordan.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV); preferred by Origen (Commentary on John 6.40); Metzger reports it in some later manuscripts and the Old Syriac

why: "Bethany" is the reading of every major edition, the Byzantine text included. Origen says that almost all copies of his day read "Bethany", but that he chose "Bethabara" because a place of that name was shown on the Jordan and he knew of no Bethany there. His influence spread the change.

p: SBLGNT, followed here, reads "Chosen One"; NA28, the Tyndale House GNT and the KJV read "Son of God."

readings.w: SBLGNT. As reported by Metzger: probably Papyrus 5, Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), some Old Latin manuscripts and the Old Syriac; Comfort adds Papyrus 106 (probably)
NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV). As reported by Metzger: Papyrus 66, Papyrus 75, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus and most manuscripts
A few Old Latin manuscripts and one Syriac version combine the two, as reported by Metzger

why: "Son of God" has more and older Greek manuscripts. But "Chosen One" is the harder reading: scribes were far more likely to change a rare title to the familiar "Son of God", which John uses often (1:49; 11:27; 20:31), than the reverse, and the combined reading "chosen Son" shows both were known early. Brown, Ehrman, Comfort and the SBLGNT editors favor "Chosen One", and the NIV (2011) and NRSVue adopted it; the NA28 and Tyndale House editors kept "Son".
b: Either title fits the scene. "Son" matches the voice from heaven at the baptism in the other Gospels (Mark 1:11). "Chosen One" matches Isaiah 42:1, where God's chosen servant receives his Spirit, as Jesus has just done.

p: The KJV has "Come and see," as Philip says in 1:46. Most editions here read a future, "you will see."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "Come and see")

why: The future is the reading of the critical editions. The command "see" matches the familiar phrase in 1:46 and 11:34, which copyists likely borrowed. The future makes Jesus' words a promise, which John develops in 1:50–51.

p: Did Andrew find Simon "first" (before anything else), "as the first one," or "early in the morning"?

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "He first findeth"); Metzger reports it also in Sinaiticus (first hand)
A few Old Latin manuscripts, as reported by Metzger

why: The adverb is the reading of all the critical editions. "The first one" may imply that the other disciple then found his own brother (some suggest James, brother of John son of Zebedee). The Latin "morning" reading may come from a Greek prōi, which looks like prōton, and would make 1:39–41 run into a new day.

t: Son of John or son of Jonah?
p: The KJV has "Simon the son of Jona." Most editions read "son of John," here and in 21:15–17.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: "John" is the reading of all the critical editions. Copyists likely changed it to "Jonah" to match Matthew 16:17, where Jesus calls him "Simon Bar-Jonah". Jonah may be a short form of the Hebrew Yohanan (John), or Simon's father may have had two names.

a: you will see heaven standing open
p: The KJV reads "Hereafter ye shall see heaven open." The critical editions lack "from now on."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.plain: you will see heaven standing open

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "Hereafter")
readings.orig: ἀπ’ ἄρτι ὄψεσθε τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγότα
readings.en: from now on you will see heaven opened
readings.plain: from now on you will see heaven standing open

why: The shorter text is printed by every critical edition. "From now on" probably came in from Jesus' words at his trial in Matthew 26:64.

a: When the wine was running short, the mother of Jesus said to him
t: A longer reading in Codex Sinaiticus
p: The first hand of Sinaiticus says the wedding's wine was used up before Mary spoke.

readings.w: All editions (SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine, Textus Receptus)
readings.orig: ὑστερήσαντος οἴνου λέγει ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πρὸς αὐτόν
readings.en: when wine ran short, the mother of Jesus says to him
readings.plain: When the wine was running short, the mother of Jesus said to him

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand) and some Old Latin manuscripts, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: οἶνον οὐκ εἶχον, ὅτι συνετελέσθη ὁ οἶνος τοῦ γάμου· εἶτα λέγει ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ
readings.en: they had no wine, because the wine of the wedding was used up; then the mother of Jesus says
readings.plain: They had no wine, because the wine for the wedding had been used up. Then the mother of Jesus said to him

why: No edition prints the longer reading. It looks like an explanation added by a copyist to make the situation clear.

p: The KJV's "hath eaten me up" follows the psalm's past tense; the editions of John have the future.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV "hath eaten me up"), matching the Septuagint of Psalm 69:9

why: Even the Byzantine text has the future, which is the harder reading, since the psalm has a past tense. The Textus Receptus brought it into line with the psalm.

p: The KJV adds "which is in heaven": the Son of Man would be in heaven while speaking on earth.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort. As reported by Metzger: Papyrus 66, Papyrus 75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, L and others

Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "even the Son of man which is in heaven"). As reported by Metzger: Alexandrinus, Θ, Ψ, families 1 and 13, most later manuscripts, the Old Latin and Vulgate
readings.orig: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ
readings.en: the Son of Man, who is in heaven
readings.plain: the Son of Man, who is in heaven.

why: The shorter text has the oldest Greek witnesses, including both early papyri. The longer reading is old and widespread, and because it is the harder reading some scholars have argued that it is original. The UBS committee, as Metzger reports, judged it an early comment added to stress the Son's heavenly origin, and most editors agree.

a: so that each one who believes may have eternal life in him.
p: The KJV repeats "should not perish" from 3:16 here. The critical editions do not.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (the Tyndale House GNT also lacks the added words, with another form of "in him")
readings.orig: ἵνα πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων ἐν αὐτῷ ἔχῃ ζωὴν αἰώνιον
readings.en: so that everyone who believes may have eternal life in him
readings.plain: so that each one who believes may have eternal life in him.

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ἵνα πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων εἰς αὐτὸν μὴ ἀπόληται, ἀλλ’ ἔχῃ ζωὴν αἰώνιον
readings.en: so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life
readings.plain: so that each one who believes in him would not be lost but would have eternal life.

why: Metzger reports that the earliest witnesses lack "may not perish but", which was copied in from the next verse. "In him" (en autō) is unusual with "believe" in John, so it most likely goes with "have eternal life": life is found in him.

p: The KJV says the argument was "with the Jews." The editions say "with a Jew," one man.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text. Metzger reports Papyrus 75, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus and most manuscripts
Textus Receptus (KJV "the Jews"). Metzger reports Papyrus 66, Sinaiticus (first hand), Θ, family 1, the Old Latin and Curetonian Syriac

why: Both readings are early. The singular is better supported and is harder, since John nearly always speaks of "the Jews" in the plural; copyists would tend to change it to the usual form. Some scholars have guessed that the original read "with Jesus' disciples" or "with Jesus", but no manuscript has that.

a: he does not give the Spirit
p: The KJV says "God giveth not the Spirit by measure." Most editions do not name the giver.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort. Metzger reports Papyrus 66, Papyrus 75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and others
readings.orig: οὐ γὰρ ἐκ μέτρου δίδωσιν τὸ πνεῦμα
readings.en: for he does not give the Spirit by measure
readings.plain: he does not give the Spirit

readings.w: Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV). Metzger reports Alexandrinus, Θ, Ψ and most later manuscripts
readings.orig: οὐ γὰρ ἐκ μέτρου δίδωσιν ὁ θεὸς τὸ πνεῦμα
readings.en: for God does not give the Spirit by measure
readings.plain: God does not give the Spirit

why: The shorter text has the earliest witnesses. Copyists added "God" to make clear who gives; the shorter text leaves open whether God gives the Spirit to the Son or the Son gives it to others (see the note).

p: The editions split: SBLGNT and NA28 say "Jesus"; the Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles and the KJV say "the Lord."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28. As reported by Metzger: Papyrus 66 (first hand), Sinaiticus, Bezae, Θ, family 1, the Old Latin and the Sinaitic and Curetonian Syriac

Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "the Lord knew"). As reported by Metzger: Papyrus 66 (corrector), Papyrus 75, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi, L, Washington (supplement), family 13 and most later manuscripts

why: The witnesses are evenly split, and so are the editions. "The Lord" has the two oldest complete papyri and Vaticanus, and the Tyndale House editors (2017) chose it. The NA28 and SBLGNT editors chose "Jesus", partly because John's narrator rarely calls Jesus "the Lord" before the resurrection (only in 6:23 and 11:2, both doubted by some), so a copyist might have introduced it to avoid saying "Jesus" twice in one sentence. This translation follows SBLGNT, but the case is close.

a: (For Jews do not share vessels with Samaritans.)
p: A few manuscripts lack the remark about Jews and Samaritans.

readings.w: All editions (SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine, Textus Receptus); Metzger reports nearly all manuscripts, including the earliest papyri
readings.en: for Jews do not share things with Samaritans
readings.plain: (For Jews do not share vessels with Samaritans.)

readings.w: As reported by Metzger: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Bezae, several Old Latin manuscripts and one Coptic version

why: The aside is in nearly all manuscripts. A few copyists may have dropped it as not literally true (the disciples were buying food from Samaritans), or as a needless comment. Metzger judges it original.

p: Goes with the end of 4:35. The KJV reads "white already to harvest. And he that reapeth..."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 (punctuation placing "already" at the start of 4:36, with no "and")
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "they are white already to harvest. And he that reapeth"), which add "and" and so attach "already" to 4:35

why: The early manuscripts are not punctuated, so the place of "already" is an editor's choice. John often puts "already" at the start of a clause (4:51; 9:22), and the Byzantine "and" looks like a later smoothing. In the Byzantine reading 4:35 ends "white already for harvest".

p: The KJV reads "the Christ, the Saviour of the world." The critical editions lack "the Christ."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ὁ σωτὴρ τοῦ κόσμου ὁ Χριστός
readings.en: the savior of the world, the Christ
readings.plain: the Savior of the world, the Messiah

why: All the critical editions omit "the Christ", which Metzger reports is missing in the earliest manuscripts. Copyists likely added it to echo the woman's question in 4:29.

a: saying that his boy was alive.
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV quote the slaves directly: "Thy son liveth."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: λέγοντες ὅτι ὁ παῖς αὐτοῦ ζῇ
readings.plain: saying that his boy was alive.

readings.w: Tregelles
readings.orig: καὶ ἀπήγγειλαν λέγοντες ὅτι ὁ παῖς αὐτοῦ ζῇ
readings.en: and reported, saying that his boy lives
readings.plain: and told him that his boy was alive.

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "and told him, saying, Thy son liveth")
readings.orig: καὶ ἀπήγγειλαν λέγοντες ὅτι ὁ παῖς σου ζῇ
readings.en: and reported, saying, Your boy lives
readings.plain: and told him, "Your boy is alive."

why: The shorter indirect form is printed by most critical editions. "And reported" and the direct speech ("your boy") look like additions that make the scene livelier and echo Jesus' words in 4:50 and 4:53. The KJV renders pais (boy) as "son". The meaning does not change.
